lines: The first time the Rus met the Mongols was in twelve twenty-three, at a river called the Kalka.
The princes of Kievan Rus rode out together for once. And it went... very badly.
[wincing] Their first team-building exercise. Total disaster.
Then the Mongols vanished back into the steppe. For fourteen years, nothing.
And in twelve thirty-seven, they came back. This time, led by Batu Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan.
City after city fell. Ryazan. Vladimir. In twelve forty, the jewel of the whole land, Kyiv, was burned to the ground.
[quietly] Remember Kyiv? The rich city on the trade road? Gone.
The Mongols didn't stay to rule the forests themselves. They set up a state on the Volga called the Golden Horde... and turned the Russian princes into their tax collectors.
If you wanted to rule a Russian city, you had to travel thousands of kilometres to the Khan, bow, bring gifts... and ask for a permission slip.
[nervous] Great Khan, I humbly ask to rule my little city.
This lasted about two hundred and forty years. Russians call it the Mongol yoke.
And here's the twist. One small, unimportant town got very good at this game: Moscow.
Its prince, Ivan the First, collected the Khan's taxes so well that people called him Ivan Kalita. Ivan Moneybag.
[holding up a coin pouch] Great nickname. Terrible for your popularity.
Moscow kept a slice of the money, bought up land, and slowly swallowed its neighbours. The head of the Church even moved there.
Moscow had learned the Mongols' best lesson: one ruler, total control, and everyone pays.
In thirteen eighty, a Moscow prince, Dmitry Donskoy, beat a Mongol army at Kulikovo Field. The Horde came back two years later and burned Moscow anyway.
[sighing] One step forward, one city on fire.
The real end came in fourteen eighty, under Ivan the Third. A Mongol army and a Moscow army met on opposite banks of the Ugra River... and stared at each other. For weeks.
Then the Mongols turned around and went home. No great battle. The yoke just... ended.
Ivan the Third tripled Moscow's land. He married Sophia, niece of the last emperor of Constantinople, and took the empire's symbol: the double-headed eagle.
Moscow now called itself the Third Rome. Chaos had produced... total control. Again.

lines: Ivan the Fourth became ruler of Moscow when he was three years old.
When he was seven, his mother died suddenly. Many believed she was poisoned.
For years, rival noble families, the boyars, fought over the boy and the palace. Ivan later wrote that they ignored him, stole from the treasury, and sometimes didn't even feed him.
[grim] This is not going to end well.
In fifteen forty-seven, at sixteen, Ivan did something new. He had himself crowned Tsar. From the Roman word Caesar.
And at first, he was... actually good. New laws, a standing army, and big wins: he conquered the Tatar cities of Kazan and Astrakhan, opening the whole Volga to Moscow.
To celebrate Kazan, he built the famous colourful cathedral on Red Square: Saint Basil's.
[pointing at the domes] That one. The one that looks like a bowl of ice cream.
Then, in fifteen sixty, his beloved wife Anastasia died. Ivan was sure she had been poisoned. And something in him broke.
He created the Oprichnina: a private police force dressed in black, riding with a dog's head and a broom on their saddles.
[whispering] The dog's head meant "we sniff out traitors". The broom meant "we sweep them away".
They terrorised the country. In fifteen seventy, Ivan's men massacred thousands in the city of Novgorod, on suspicion of treason.
Then came the worst moment of all. In fifteen eighty-one, during a furious argument, Ivan struck his own son and heir with his iron-tipped staff.
The young man died days later. Ivan never recovered from it.
[timid] Your Majesty... the ambassador from England is here.
When Ivan died in fifteen eighty-four, Russia was bigger than ever. Even Siberia had begun to open, thanks to a Cossack adventurer called Yermak.
But the country was exhausted, terrified, and broke. And the next tsar, Ivan's son Feodor, was gentle, pious... and had no children.
[checking his watch] Total control went too far. You know what comes next.
Feodor died in fifteen ninety-eight. And with him, the family of Rurik, after more than seven hundred years, was gone.
Russians literally named the next fifteen years the Time of Troubles.
First, a powerful noble called Boris Godunov grabbed the throne. Then the weather turned against him.
Around sixteen hundred and one, frosts and rain wrecked the harvest three years in a row. A terrible famine killed a huge part of the population.
And then a young man appeared in Poland with an incredible claim.
[grandly] I am Dmitry, the lost son of Ivan the Terrible!
[doubtful] Didn't Dmitry die as a child?
The real Dmitry had died in fifteen ninety-one. But the False Dmitry marched on Moscow with Polish support, and when Boris suddenly died, Moscow let him in. He was crowned tsar.
Within a year, angry boyars killed him. The story goes that his body was burned, and his ashes were fired from a cannon back towards Poland.
[covering his eyes] That's one way to return to sender.
Then came another tsar. Then a second False Dmitry. Then the Swedes invaded. Then, in sixteen ten, the Polish army marched into Moscow and took the Kremlin itself.
Russia had no tsar, no government, and a foreign army in its heart.
And then, something unusual happened. Ordinary people fixed it.
In the city of Nizhny Novgorod, a meat trader named Kuzma Minin started collecting money for a people's army, and asked a wounded prince, Dmitry Pozharsky, to lead it.
In sixteen twelve, they drove the Poles out of Moscow. Russia still celebrates that day as a national holiday.
[impressed] A butcher saving the country. Respect.
In sixteen thirteen, an assembly chose a new tsar: a shy sixteen-year-old named Michael Romanov.
His family would rule Russia for the next three hundred and four years.
Chaos, again, had produced order. The loop was complete. Time for the next one.

lines: Peter was born in sixteen seventy-two.
At ten, he became co-tsar with his half-brother, while his older sister Sophia actually ran things.
That same year, rebel palace guards, the Streltsy, stormed the Kremlin, and young Peter watched them kill members of his mother's family in front of him.
Peter grew up outside the palace, playing war games with real soldiers and real cannons. He grew to over two metres tall. Around six foot eight.
[looking up, way up] He had to duck through most doorways in Russia.
In sixteen ninety-seven, he did something no tsar had ever done. He went to Western Europe himself, in disguise, as "Peter Mikhailov".
He worked as a carpenter in Dutch shipyards, studied English factories, and fell in love with everything modern.
You're seven feet tall and fifty men follow you everywhere.
Back home, he started changing Russia by force. He ordered his nobles to shave their beards. He cut some off himself, with scissors.
If you really wanted to keep your beard, you paid a beard tax, and carried a token to prove it.
[stroking his chin] Imagine needing a licence for your face.
European clothes. A new calendar, with New Year on January the first. Schools for maths and navigation. A real navy.
He fought Sweden for twenty-one years. He lost badly at Narva in seventeen hundred... then smashed the Swedes at Poltava in seventeen oh nine.
Now Russia had what it always wanted: a way to the Baltic Sea.
And on a swamp by that sea, Peter built a brand new capital: Saint Petersburg. Thousands of forced labourers died building it.
He made himself Emperor. Russia was now an empire.
But Peter's total control reached his own family. His son Alexei hated the reforms and fled abroad.
Peter lured him home with promises, then had him put on trial. Alexei died in prison in seventeen eighteen.
[quietly] That's the second tsar in this story to lose his son by his own hand.
Peter then made a new law: the emperor could pick any heir he liked. And in seventeen twenty-five, he died... without picking anyone.
For the next thirty-seven years, Russia had a strange system: whoever the palace guards liked, became ruler.
Empresses, a child emperor, regents: one palace coup after another.
In seventeen forty-four, a teenage German princess named Sophie arrived in Russia to marry the heir to the throne, Peter.
She learned Russian. She converted to Orthodoxy. She took a new name: Catherine.
Her husband, meanwhile, preferred playing with toy soldiers and openly worshipped Russia's enemy, the King of Prussia.
In seventeen sixty-two, he became Peter the Third, and immediately handed back everything Russia had won from Prussia in a long, bloody war.
[stunned] He won the game, then gave the other team the trophy.
Your Majesty, the guards are... unhappy with your husband.
[standing, smiling] Then I suppose I should get dressed.
Six months into his reign, Catherine and the guards overthrew him. A week later, Peter was dead. The official cause, the story goes, was a "stomach problem".

Catherine the Second ruled for thirty-four years. She wrote to famous French thinkers like Voltaire, collected thousands of paintings, which became the Hermitage museum, and talked about freedom and reason.
She also grabbed a lot of land. Crimea in seventeen eighty-three. Big parts of Poland, which was carved up until it disappeared from the map.
And her traders crossed the Pacific. In seventeen eighty-four, Russians built their first permanent settlement in a faraway place called... Alaska.
[checking his watch, grinning] Ooh. Remember that one. We know how this ends.
But for most Russians, life got harder. Millions of peasants were serfs, owned by landlords, bought and sold with the land.
In seventeen seventy-three, a Cossack called Pugachev claimed to be the dead Peter the Third, and led a huge peasant uprising across the Volga. It took two years to crush.
Freedom for the nobles, control for everyone else. The loop, in a powdered wig.
[to camera] By the way, if you're enjoying this, subscribe. It's free, and it makes the time machine run.
When Catherine died in seventeen ninety-six, Russia was a giant on Europe's stage.
And in the west, a short French general was about to test exactly how big that giant really was.
